This document explains the choices behind RADdiversity: how the data should
be filtered, which estimators are used and why, which Stacks file to use for
which statistic, how uncertainty is measured, and why populations are
compared with the individual, not the locus, as the unit. It is written for
readers who know what heterozygosity is but have not had to choose between
estimators before.

To see the analysis itself step by step, start with
`vignette("workflow", package = "RADdiversity")`. Text for a methods section
and answers to common reviewer questions are in
`vignette("reviewer-faq", package = "RADdiversity")`.

> **Where the numbers come from.** Simulation results quoted here can be
> re-run: Appendix C lists each one with the script or function that
> produces it (`inst/sims/` in the installed package, or a self-test
> function). Where a statement rests on the Stacks source code, the file and
> version are named.
>
> **Command line.** Every analysis can also be run from a shell with the
> scripts in `system.file("scripts", package = "RADdiversity")`, e.g.
> `Rscript diversity_stats.R populations.haps.vcf popmap.tsv --g=20`. The R
> functions are used throughout this document.

## 1. Getting the data

### Genotypes backed by few reads

A genotype is called from the reads that happened to be sequenced. If a true
heterozygote is covered by only a few reads, all of them may come from the
same chromosome, and it is called homozygous. With *d* reads the chance of
that is 2<sup>1−*d*</sup>:

| reads backing the genotype | chance a heterozygote shows only one allele |
|---|---|
| 3 | 25% |
| 5 | 6% |
| 10 | 0.2% |

Stacks' `populations --min-gt-depth 6` (Stacks 2.67 and later) sets such
genotypes to missing, as does `filter_genotype_depth(H, min_dp = 6)` in R.
The missing-data rate rises, but a visible gap is better than a hidden
error. Both treat heterozygous and homozygous calls alike, which matters: a
filter that removed heterozygotes more readily than homozygotes (as
`filter_low_conf_alt()` does) would itself bias Ho down and FIS up.

### Missing data: filter within populations

Stacks offers two missing-data filters that look alike:

- `-r 0.8 -p 2`: keep a locus if at least 80% of individuals **within each
  population** are genotyped, in at least 2 populations;
- `-R 0.8`: keep a locus if at least 80% of **all individuals pooled** are
  genotyped.

With the pooled rule, a locus can pass by being well genotyped in a large
population while mostly missing in a small one. The small population then
carries more missing data than the large one, and any effect of missing data
on heterozygosity or FIS differs between exactly the two samples being
compared. Use `-r` with `-p` equal to the number of populations, or
`filter_call_rate(H, min_call, popmap = pops)` in R.

### Allele-frequency filters

Minor allele count and frequency filters (`--min-mac`, `--min-maf`) are
standard for RAD-seq data, and useful for analyses that are sensitive to
genotyping errors in rare variants (STRUCTURE, PCA, kinship). For diversity
statistics it helps to know what they remove. Rare variants are real
diversity: under a neutral site frequency spectrum, a site whose derived
allele is carried by *i* of *N* gene copies contributes to π in proportion to
*N* − *i*, so sites with a minor allele count of 2 or less hold about 4/(*N*
− 1) of π:

| diploids in the run | share of π at sites with minor allele count ≤ 2 |
|---|---|
| 10 | 21% |
| 20 | 10% |
| 30 | 7% |

The share depends on sample size, so a MAC filter lowers per-site diversity
more in a small study than in a large one. Stacks does not delete a SNP that
fails the filter: it turns it into a fixed site (`LocusFilter::erase_snp()`,
Stacks 2.68), so the site still counts in `Sites` and the loss shows up in
Stacks' own all-positions `Pi` as well. Allelic richness and private allelic
richness lose even more, because rare alleles are what they count. None of
this makes filtered data unusable; it makes the threshold part of what a
reported value means, so state it, and compare values only between datasets
filtered the same way. If you control the pipeline, a separate unfiltered
run for diversity statistics avoids the question.

### Hardy-Weinberg filters

A Hardy-Weinberg filter removes loci with a heterozygote deficit, which is
what inbreeding produces, so it removes the signal FIS measures. Filtering
on HWE with all populations pooled is worse: differences in allele frequency
between populations look like heterozygote deficits (the Wahlund effect),
so the loci most informative about population structure are removed
(Pearman et al. 2022). RADdiversity's `hwe_test()` reports departures but
nothing in the package removes loci on them (section 7).

`--max-obs-het` is different: it removes sites where most individuals are
heterozygous, a crude screen for paralogs (two similar genomic regions
assembled as one locus), and is reasonable to use.

### Data filtered before they reach the package

Many VCFs arrive already filtered. The analyses still run; the table in
`vignette("workflow")` ("If your data were already filtered") lists what each
common filter changes and what to report, and `summary()` of a
`diversity_stats()` result shows what the data look filtered at (the rarest
allele count left, the lowest call rates, the highest per-record Ho). An HWE
filter cannot be detected from the data.

### Which records each population uses

`diversity_stats()` uses a record for a population once that population has
at least `min_n` genotyped individuals there (default 2, the smallest number
for which He and FIS are defined). This is decided for each population
separately, so an individual missing in one population does not cost the
other population that record. Because FIS is a ratio of sums over loci (next
section), loci with fewer typed individuals simply contribute less, and no
further correction is needed; `diversity_core_selftest()` checks by
simulation that FIS stays unbiased when missingness is clustered by locus, as
it is in real RAD data.

`complete_case = TRUE` uses a record only if every individual of every
population is genotyped there (Schmidt et al. 2021, recommendation (b)).
Records survive that rule at a rate of about (1 − *m*)<sup>*n*</sup> for a
missing-genotype rate *m* spread over *n* individuals, which falls quickly:

| missing rate *m* | records surviving with 25 individuals |
|---|---|
| 2% | 60% |
| 5% | 28% |
| 10% | 7% |

A small, possibly unrepresentative subset of loci is a bigger problem than
missing data handled locus by locus, so the default is the per-population
rule; use `complete_case = TRUE` as a sensitivity analysis.

## 2. The estimators

### One parameter, several names

Expected heterozygosity (He), gene diversity (Hs) and nucleotide diversity
(π) are all estimates of **one parameter**: the probability that two gene
copies drawn at random from a population differ. They differ in two ways.

* **What is averaged over.** He is usually averaged over the variant records
  a study called. π is the same quantity averaged over **every sequenced
  site**, monomorphic ones included. Because most sites are monomorphic, π is
  orders of magnitude smaller than He from the same data, and He per variant
  site depends on how many variants a study happened to call, while π does
  not.
* **Which estimator.** The plug-in 1 − Σ*p*<sup>2</sup> is biased low in
  small samples; the two usual corrections are discussed next.

There is one more distinction at haplotype loci. At a biallelic site, gene
diversity and π per site are the same thing. At a multi-allelic RAD
haplotype locus, gene diversity treats any two different haplotypes as
simply "different", while nucleotide diversity would count how many bases
differ. So on a haplotype VCF nothing is nucleotide diversity, whatever it is
called.

In RADdiversity's output, `He` is always per variant record, `He_autosomal`
(from `diversity_stats(sites = )`) and `pi_nc` (from `pi_allsites()`) are per
sequenced site.

### Why Nei & Chesser's He

For a sample of *N* diploid individuals with allele frequencies *p*<sub>i</sub>
and observed heterozygosity *H*<sub>o</sub>, three estimators are in use:

| estimator | formula | expectation, for true diversity *H* and inbreeding *F* |
|---|---|---|
| plug-in (Stacks `Exp_Het`) | 1 − Σ*p*<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> | *H* (2*N* − 1 − *F*)/(2*N*) |
| 2*N*-corrected (Stacks `Pi`) | (2*N*/(2*N* − 1))(1 − Σ*p*<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>) | *H* (1 − *F*/(2*N* − 1)) |
| Nei & Chesser (1983) | (*N*/(*N* − 1))(1 − Σ*p*<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> − *H*<sub>o</sub>/(2*N*)) | *H* |

The 2*N*-corrected estimator treats the 2*N* gene copies as independent draws,
which is true only when *F* = 0. When individuals are inbred, it runs low by
the factor *F*/(2*N* − 1), usually well under 1%. Nei & Chesser's estimator
uses *H*<sub>o</sub> to remove that dependence and is unbiased at any *F*; it
is also what hierfstat reports as Hs.

The small bias matters for FIS, which divides by He. With the 2*N*-corrected
He, FIS is pulled toward zero by roughly a factor 1/(2*N* − 1): about 3% at
*N* = 15 and 5% at *N* = 10. Because this depends on *N*, it does not cancel
when two populations of different size are compared. It also sets the wrong
limit: when every individual is heterozygous at a biallelic locus, the true
FIS is −1, but 1 − *H*<sub>o</sub>/`Pi` gives −(*N* − 1)/*N* (−0.9 at *N* =
10); the Nei & Chesser version gives −1. `diversity_core_selftest()` checks
all of this by simulation.

`diversity_stats()` reports both estimators side by side in
`estimator_comparison` (`He_NeiChesser`, `He_2n_corr`), so values from
other software can be reconciled.

### Why FIS is a ratio of sums

FIS combines thousands of loci. It can be computed per locus and then
averaged ("mean of ratios"), or computed once from the sums over loci:
FIS = 1 − ΣH<sub>o</sub>/ΣH<sub>s</sub> ("ratio of sums"). A batting average
is the everyday version: adding every hit and every at-bat gives the team's
average; averaging each player's own average counts the pitcher who batted
twice as much as the regular who batted 600 times.

Loci differ enormously in how much they say about FIS: a nearly monomorphic
locus has He near zero and a per-locus FIS that is almost pure noise. The
ratio of sums weights each locus by its He, which is the weighting used by
Weir & Cockerham (1984) and recommended for combining loci (Bhatia et al.
2013 make the same point for FST). A locus monomorphic in a population
contributes 0 to both sums, so whether such loci are included does not
change the result.

Stacks reports FIS as a mean of per-site ratios, counting sites monomorphic
in the population as 0 (`populations.cc`, Stacks 2.68), and divides by `Pi`.
Its own columns therefore do not reconcile. In the example data's
`example.sumstats_summary.tsv`, computed the same way, north's
1 − `Obs_Het`/`Pi` is 0.092 while its `Fis` column reads 0.081; for south,
0.159 against 0.106.

### Heterozygosity per sequenced site

He averaged over variant records is heterozygosity *per variant your study
called*: call more variants and it changes, so it cannot be compared with
other studies. Schmidt et al. (2021) show that the comparable quantity is
heterozygosity per sequenced site. From a SNP VCF it is one multiplication:

> He<sub>autosomal</sub> = He × (variant records) ÷ (sequenced sites)

`diversity_stats(snps, pops, g, sites = "populations.sumstats_summary.tsv")`
does this for each population separately, using that population's own
`Sites` and `Variant_Sites` from the "All positions (variant and fixed)"
block of the Stacks file. A population's own counts matter: Stacks counts a
site for a population only where it has at least one genotyped individual
(`SumStatsSummary::accumulate()`, Stacks 2.68), and with several populations
and `-p` below their number, a population can be absent from many records.

Two conditions apply. The records must be single sites, so the conversion
is done only for the SNP VCF. And every variant site must be counted in the
numerator: records removed after reading (with a `filter_*()` function) are
still in `Sites`, which is why the `Variant_Sites` count from the Stacks file
is used when available.

The rescaling cannot account for missing genotypes at monomorphic sites. An
all-sites VCF (`populations --vcf-all`) and `pi_allsites()` handle missing
data site by site instead (Korunes & Samuk 2021), and give `pi_nc`, the
per-site version of Nei & Chesser's He. With little missing data the two
agree closely, as they do in the example data.

### Per polymorphic site: use the pooled denominator

Many RAD-seq papers report He "per polymorphic site". That phrase has two
readings, and they can give opposite answers:

- **pooled**: averaged over sites variable anywhere in the dataset (what
  Stacks' "Variant positions" block and `diversity_stats()` do);
- **within-population**: for each population, averaged only over the sites
  variable in that population.

In a simulation where population B was founded by three individuals from A
(`inst/sims/vignette_sims.R`, part `denominator`), B was less diverse, but
the within-population denominator reversed the difference:

| denominator | He, population A | He, population B | ratio A:B |
|---|---|---|---|
| pooled | 0.318 | 0.265 | 1.20 |
| within-population | 0.353 | 0.391 | 0.90 |

The reason: after a bottleneck, B is monomorphic at many sites, and that is
its reduced diversity. Dropping those sites from B's denominator discards
the evidence and keeps only the sites where B retained variation. The two
versions are linked exactly by He(pooled) = He(within) × `pct_poly`/100, so
reporting the pooled He with `pct_poly` beside it lets a reader recover
either.

### Rarefied allelic and private allelic richness

The number of alleles found grows with the number of gene copies sampled, so
populations of different size must be compared at a common sample size *g*
(in gene copies). The expected number of alleles in *g* copies drawn without
replacement from a population's *N* copies is

> A(*g*) = Σ<sub>i</sub> [1 − C(*N* − *N*<sub>i</sub>, *g*)/C(*N*, *g*)]

(Hurlbert 1971; El Mousadik & Petit 1996), where *N*<sub>i</sub> is the count
of allele *i*. Private allelic richness is the expected number of alleles
drawn in one population and in none of the others, each sampled to *g*
copies (Kalinowski 2004; Szpiech et al. 2008).

Both are exact expectations over gene copies, as in HP-RARE and ADZE.
Resampling *individuals* instead would estimate something different when
individuals are inbred, because the two copies inside one individual are not
independent draws.

**Choosing *g*.** A locus counts for a population only where it has at
least *g* gene copies, and for private richness only where *every*
population does. A large *g* therefore discards loci with missing data:
compare `Ar_n` and `privAr_n` for two values of *g*
(`vignette("workflow")`, section 5) and choose the largest *g* that keeps
most loci. Private richness depends on how many other populations it is
compared against, so it cannot be compared between studies with different
numbers of populations.

## 3. Which Stacks file for which statistic

Stacks writes one record per SNP (`populations.snps.vcf`) and one record per
RAD locus with haplotype alleles (`populations.haps.vcf`).

| statistic | file | reason |
|---|---|---|
| Ho, He, He per sequenced site | SNP VCF | a per-SNP value means the same in every study |
| FIS | haplotype VCF | a ratio, so the scale cancels; more information per locus |
| rarefied allelic richness | haplotype VCF | at a biallelic SNP it can only be 1 or 2 |
| rarefied private allelic richness | haplotype VCF | the same, though it is informative on SNPs too |
| tests between populations | either; say which | |

### FIS from haplotypes

A RAD locus with three SNPs becomes one marker with up to eight alleles, and
multi-allelic markers carry more information about the heterozygote deficit.
Biallelic SNPs also have a specific weakness: a minor allele present in a
single copy must sit in a heterozygote, which forces Ho = He and FIS = 0 at
that site by arithmetic.

In simulations with a known FIS of 0.10 (`vignette_sims.R`, part
`file_choice`; *n* = 15 and 10, 1,200 RAD loci, 20 replicates), all three
kinds of file were unbiased, and the haplotype file gave the narrowest
interval:

| data | FIS | width of the 95% interval | records |
|---|---|---|---|
| haplotype VCF | 0.099 | 0.028 | 1,200 |
| all SNPs | 0.099 | 0.031 | 2,251 |
| one SNP per RAD locus | 0.098 | 0.035 | 1,200 |

In this simulation, identity by descent is drawn once per individual per RAD
locus, as real inbreeding acts on whole haplotypes. Drawing it separately
for each SNP would make haplotype homozygosity too low and the haplotype
file look worse than it is.

### Ho and He from SNPs

Haplotype gene diversity has no fixed ceiling: a locus with four SNPs can
carry many haplotypes, a locus with one SNP only two. Haplotype He therefore
depends on read length, enzyme and SNP-calling settings. In simulations that
varied only the number of SNPs per locus (`vignette_sims.R`, part
`snp_density`), haplotype He changed by 66% across the range and per-SNP He
by 24% (part of which is real, because loci with more SNPs are more
variable). Both files gave the same ratio between two populations (1.14), so
either can compare populations within one study; only the SNP values can be
compared with other studies.

**Ho and He are not comparable between the two files.** Haplotype Ho asks "is
this RAD locus heterozygous?", which is true if *any* of its SNPs is; per-SNP
Ho asks it of one site. In the same simulation Ho was 0.42 from haplotypes
and 0.32 from SNPs for the same individuals. Label every table with the file
its numbers came from. FIS, a ratio, is comparable, and FIS from the two
files should agree closely; if it does not, likely causes are sequencing
errors creating spurious rare haplotypes (lowering haplotype FIS), or
haplotype genotypes going missing more often in heterozygotes (Stacks writes
a whole haplotype as missing if any of its SNPs is uncalled;
`export_formats.cc`, Stacks 2.68), raising haplotype FIS.

### Linked SNPs and thinning

SNPs on one RAD locus are physically linked and are not independent
replicates. RADdiversity handles this by resampling whole RAD loci for every
standard error and interval (section 4), so linked SNPs move together.
Thinning to one SNP per locus is then unnecessary for these statistics and
discards data, as the table above shows. Analyses that assume unlinked
markers (STRUCTURE, PCA, some Ne estimators) do need a thinned dataset; for
those, a random SNP per locus (`--write-random-snp`, or
`filter_thin_one_snp(method = "random")`) is better than the first, which
always sits at the same position relative to the cut site.

## 4. Uncertainty

### Resampling RAD loci

Every standard error and interval in `diversity_stats()`,
`differentiation_stats()` and `pi_allsites()` resamples whole RAD loci:

* `_se` columns: a delete-one-locus jackknife (Weir 1996). Each RAD locus is
  left out in turn and the statistic recomputed; no random numbers are used.
* `_lo`/`_hi` columns: a 95% percentile bootstrap, drawing RAD loci with
  replacement.

Resampling SNP rows instead would treat linked SNPs as independent and give
intervals that are too narrow. hierfstat's `boot.ppfis()` and Stacks'
`StdErr` columns both resample or average over individual SNP rows.

### Loci or individuals: which uncertainty?

Locus-based intervals hold the sampled individuals fixed: they answer "what
if I had typed different loci in these animals?". With many loci and
individuals that are alike, that is close to the full uncertainty, because
the variation from which individuals were sampled averages away across loci
(Nei & Roychoudhury 1974; Nei 1978). When individuals differ in inbreeding, it
does not: an inbred individual is homozygous at many loci at once, and adding
loci does not remove that. `inst/sims/coverage_se.R` measures how often
estimate ± 1.96 SE contains the true value (two populations of 15, 1,000
loci, mean F = 0.1, 200 replicates):

| SD of F among individuals | statistic | locus SE (`_se`) | individual SE (`_se_ind`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Ho | 98.8% | 94.2% |
| 0 | FIS | 95.5% | 94.2% |
| 0.10 | Ho | 65.5% | 94.5% |
| 0.10 | FIS | 54.2% | 93.0% |
| 0.25 | Ho | 37.0% | 93.0% |
| 0.25 | FIS | 27.5% | 93.5% |

The rule that follows:

1. Estimate g2 (`identity_disequilibrium()`; also in `het_between_pops()`),
   which is 0 when individuals do not differ in inbreeding (David et al.
   2007).
2. If its interval includes 0, the locus-based `_se`, `_lo` and `_hi` are
   appropriate.
3. If it excludes 0, report the delete-one-individual jackknife standard
   errors from `diversity_stats(..., se_individuals = TRUE)`.
4. Either way, compare populations with `het_between_pops()`, not by
   whether intervals overlap.

### Individual standard errors for Ar and privAr

The individual jackknife is less reliable for the two rarefied statistics
(`inst/sims/jackknife_richness.R`: two populations of 10, 3,000 loci with four
alleles, 200 replicates per row). The table gives the average reported
`_se_ind` divided by the true standard error of the estimate (1 is right).
"Near g" is the share of a population's records with a defined Ar that have
fewer than *g* + 2 gene copies.

| missing genotypes | *g* | near *g* | Ar | privAr | He | FIS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0% | 10 | 0% | 1.21 | 0.78 | 1.10 | 1.06 |
| 0% | 18 | 0% | 1.23 | 0.93 | 1.04 | 0.95 |
| 1% | 18 | 9% | 1.28 | 0.91 | 0.95 | 0.97 |
| 3% | 18 | 24% | 1.58 | 1.24 | 1.09 | 1.00 |
| 10% | 10 | 0.1% | 1.20 | 0.86 | 1.14 | 1.04 |
| 10% | 12 | 1% | 1.27 | 0.93 | 1.09 | 1.02 |
| 10% | 14 | 6% | 1.40 | 0.90 | 1.05 | 1.10 |
| 10% | 16 | 21% | 1.53 | 1.05 | 1.00 | 1.06 |
| 10% | 18 | 53% | 2.01 | 1.80 | 0.98 | 1.03 |

Two things go wrong. First, `privAr_se_ind` deletes only the population's
own individuals, but private richness also depends on which individuals were
sampled in the *other* populations, which it holds fixed; it runs too small,
by up to about 20%. Second, at a record with fewer than *g* + 2 gene copies,
deleting one individual leaves fewer than *g*, so the record drops out of
some jackknife replicates and not others. Those replicates then average over
different records, and both SEs grow, to about twice the true value when half
the records sit there. `diversity_stats()` warns when more than 5% of a
population's records do, and names a smaller *g* to use for these two SEs.
The Ar SE otherwise runs about 20% large, as delete-one jackknife variances
tend to. He and FIS individual SEs were accurate in every setting.

### Why not bootstrap individuals?

`diversity_stats(boot = "individuals")` resamples individuals within each
population (as diveRsity's `divBasic()` does), and `boot = "both"` resamples
individuals and loci (Owen & Eckles 2012). Both are kept only for comparison
with other software, because their intervals miss the true value far too
often (`vignette_sims.R`, part `boot_modes`; biallelic loci with fixed
frequencies, F = 0.1, 150 replicates):

| | n = 10: He | n = 10: FIS | n = 15: He | n = 15: FIS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `boot = "loci"` | 99% | 95% | 99% | 96% |
| `boot = "individuals"` | 0% | 5% | 0% | 5% |
| `boot = "both"` | 1% | 14% | 3% | 26% |

(The locus bootstrap covers He more than 95% of the time here because the
simulation keeps the same loci in every replicate, while the bootstrap also
includes variation among loci.)

The reason is specific to these estimators. Nei & Chesser's He and the
rarefaction formulas include small-sample corrections that assume the *n*
individuals are distinct. A bootstrap sample drawn with replacement contains
on average only about 63% distinct individuals, the corrections cannot know
that, and the resampled values are systematically biased low. The bias does
not shrink with more loci while the bootstrap spread does, so the intervals
end up centered in the wrong place. A jackknife over individuals leaves
individuals out rather than duplicating them, which is why it is the
individual-level standard error offered.

For reference, diveRsity's `divBasic()` resamples individuals and computes
He as the uncorrected 1 − Σ*p*<sup>2</sup> (GitHub source, `R/divBasic.R`),
so its intervals describe a different, plug-in estimator.

### Stacks' StdErr columns

Stacks' `populations.sumstats_summary.tsv` reports `StdErr` as the standard
deviation over variant sites divided by √(number of sites)
(`SumStatsSummary::final_calculation()`, Stacks 2.68). That treats every SNP
as independent, so it is narrower than an interval over RAD loci. In Stacks
2.68 the `StdErr` printed for `Fis` is computed from `Num_Indv`'s variance
(`populations.cc`, line 3108), apparently a copy-and-paste slip; check it
against your own Stacks version before relying on that column.

## 5. Comparing populations

### Why loci are the wrong replicates

A common way to compare heterozygosity between populations is to bootstrap
over loci, or to run a paired test on per-locus values. Both treat loci as
the replicates. But every locus is measured on the same few individuals, and
the quantity of interest, a population mean, is uncertain mainly because of
which individuals were sampled. A locus-based interval shrinks as
1/√(number of loci) while that uncertainty does not, so with thousands of
loci it becomes far too narrow.

`het_between_pops_selftest()` simulates two populations with *identical*
true heterozygosity (n = 15 and 10, 1,500 loci), so every significant result
is a false positive. With a nominal 5% rate, a locus bootstrap rejected about
8% of the time when individuals did not differ in inbreeding, about half the
time when the SD of F among individuals was 0.10, and about 80% of the time
at 0.25. Welch's *t* on one heterozygosity value per individual stayed near
5% throughout. The objection is not new: Van Dongen (1995) made it for
allozyme data, and Petit & Pons (1998) repeated it.

### The test on individuals

`het_between_pops()` gives each individual one number, its heterozygosity
over the loci its population clears `min_call` at, and compares populations
with Welch's *t*-test (which does not assume equal variances), with the
Wilcoxon rank-sum test as a check that does not assume normality. It reports
the difference with its confidence interval and Hedges' *g*, the difference
in units of the among-individual standard deviation.

Two questions use the same machinery. Mean individual heterozygosity asks
whether populations differ in **diversity**. The individual inbreeding
coefficient F = 1 − (observed heterozygous loci)/(expected), with the
expectation from the individual's own population, asks whether they differ in
**inbreeding**; its population mean equals FIS when every individual is typed
at every locus (`?individual_inbreeding`).

With three or more populations, report the overall test first (`omnibus`:
Welch's one-way ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis), then the pairwise tests with
Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values.

### Checks before reporting

* **Relatives.** Relatives are not independent individuals, and one family
  can dominate a small sample; screen with `kinship_check()` (section 7).
* **Missing data.** If poorly sequenced individuals are both more often
  missing and, through allele dropout, more often called homozygous, a
  difference between populations can be a difference in library quality.
  `het_between_pops()` correlates each individual's call rate with its
  heterozygosity and flags a positive correlation.
* **Overdispersion.** The ratio of the observed variance of individual
  heterozygosity to its binomial expectation shows how far a locus-based test
  would have been from correct on *these* data.
* **Power.** Power is set by the number of individuals, not loci. With 15
  and 10 individuals and an among-individual SD of F of 0.10, Welch's test
  detected a difference in mean F of 0.05 (0.5 SD) 17% of the time and of
  0.08 (0.8 SD) 39% of the time (`vignette_sims.R`, part `power`). A
  non-significant result from such samples is weak evidence of no
  difference; write "no difference was detected".

### Null alleles and allele dropout

A mutation in a restriction site stops a chromosome from producing reads, so
its carrier looks homozygous for its other allele, or is missing if both
copies drop out. This "allele dropout" inflates FIS. It is also more common
at more variable loci and in more diverse populations (Gautier et al. 2013;
Arnold et al. 2013), so it does not affect every population equally: it can
understate a real difference in He, and it can create a difference in FIS.

Depth filters do not remove it. `diversity_stats()` returns
`fis_by_call_rate`, which groups each population's loci by its own call rate
there: dropout makes FIS rise as call rate falls, while inbreeding raises FIS
at every locus alike. If FIS rises, report FIS from well-typed loci
(`complete_case = TRUE` or a higher `min_n`) as well.

## 6. Differentiation

### FST

`differentiation_stats()` computes Weir & Cockerham's (1984) FST from its
variance components *a*, *b* and *c*, summed over loci before taking the
ratio (FST = Σ*a*/Σ(*a* + *b* + *c*)), for all populations and for each pair.
The implementation matches `hierfstat::wc()` to machine precision on records
typed in at least two of the compared populations (package tests).

One choice differs from hierfstat. A record where only one of the compared
populations has any genotyped individual says nothing about differences
between them, yet its within-population variance would enter the
denominator and pull FST toward 0. Such records are common with three or
more populations and `-p` below their number. RADdiversity skips them, as
VCFtools and Stacks' own pairwise FST do; `hierfstat::wc()` keeps them. The
number skipped is in `settings$fst_records_skipped`.

### Jost's D and beta

FST cannot reach 1 when loci are highly variable, even for populations that
share no alleles, so FST from many-haplotype RAD loci is not comparable with
FST from SNPs. Jost's (2008) D is built to avoid that ceiling. D is computed
from Hs and Ht averaged over loci (not by averaging per-locus D), following
the formula as implemented in the mmod package (Winter 2012; see
`inst/NOTICE`). Its correction of Hs uses 2*N*/(2*N* − 1), which assumes
random mating, so with a heterozygote deficit D is biased slightly upward.
Weir & Goudet's (2017) beta, via hierfstat, is a third measure; it is a point
estimate only, and slow on large datasets (`beta = FALSE` skips it).

**The global D uses only records genotyped in every population.** Jost's D
for *k* populations measures differentiation among those *k* populations. A
record where some of them are untyped measures it among a different, smaller
set, and averaging such records in biases the global D: for three completely
differentiated populations (true D = 1), one of them untyped at half the
records, it came out at 0.875 (package tests). So the global D skips those
records, and `D_records` in the result, `print()` and `summary()` report how
many records it rests on. Each pairwise D uses every record typed in both of
its populations, and FST uses every record typed in at least two
populations, because Weir & Cockerham's estimator handles a varying number of
populations per record.

Report D (or beta) alongside FST for haplotype data. Intervals for FST and D
come from the same bootstrap over RAD loci as everything else.

## 7. Relatives and Hardy-Weinberg tests

### Screening for relatives

`kinship_check()` estimates kinship for every pair with KING-robust
(Manichaikul et al. 2010), which uses no allele frequencies and so is not
misled by population structure, or with Goudet's beta (Goudet, Kay & Weir
2018) via hierfstat. A benchmark on reduced-representation data from
non-model species (McMaster et al. 2025) found KING precise but insensitive
(it misses many true relatives) and beta sensitive but imprecise, worse under
structure and inbreeding. Treat both as screens: a flagged pair deserves a
look, and an empty list is not proof there are no relatives.

Two details. The package uses Manichaikul et al.'s estimator with the
**sum** of the two individuals' heterozygote counts in the denominator; PLINK
2's `--make-king` uses their between-family version (the smaller count),
which reads lower when one individual's heterozygotes were under-called.
And beta compares each pair with the average pair it is given, so on several
differentiated populations pooled, unrelated members of the same population
look related; with `popmap`, beta is computed within each population.

### Hardy-Weinberg tests

`hwe_test()` runs the exact test of Hardy-Weinberg proportions (Levene 1949;
Haldane 1954): exactly, by listing every possible table, for biallelic loci
(the test PLINK and VCFtools use; Wigginton et al. 2005), and by Guo &
Thompson's (1992) direct Monte Carlo method for multi-allelic haplotype loci,
stopping early once a p-value is clearly not small (Besag & Clifford 1991).
Each locus gets `F`, the direction of any departure. It is a report, never a
filter (section 1). Loci with a heterozygote excess in every population are
candidate paralogs worth inspecting.

## Appendix A. Stacks columns and RADdiversity

Notation: *N* diploid individuals genotyped at a site, 2*N* gene copies,
allele frequencies *p*<sub>i</sub>, observed heterozygosity *H*<sub>o</sub>.

| quantity | formula | Stacks column | RADdiversity |
|---|---|---|---|
| observed heterozygosity | heterozygotes / *N* | `Obs_Het` | `Ho` |
| gene diversity, plug-in | 1 − Σ*p*<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> | `Exp_Het` | not reported |
| gene diversity, 2*N*-corrected | (2*N*/(2*N* − 1))(1 − Σ*p*<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>) | `Pi` | `He_2n_corr` |
| gene diversity, Nei & Chesser | (*N*/(*N* − 1))(1 − Σ*p*<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> − *H*<sub>o</sub>/(2*N*)) | not available | `He` |
| FIS at a site | 1 − *H*<sub>o</sub>/(gene diversity) | `Fis`, using `Pi` | not reported per site |
| FIS over sites | mean of per-site FIS (Stacks); 1 − Σ*H*<sub>o</sub>/Σ*H*<sub>s</sub> (RADdiversity) | `Fis` | `Fis` |
| per-site diversity | mean over all sequenced sites | `Pi`, All-positions block | `He_autosomal`, `pi_nc` |
| private alleles | raw count | `Private` | `privAr` (rarefied) |

Stacks' `Pi` estimates the same parameter as `He` and differs from it by
about *F*/(2*N* − 1); `diversity_stats()` prints both. Its `Fis` differs from
RADdiversity's in both the denominator (`Pi`) and the averaging (section 2).
The per-site `Pi` in the "Variant positions" block is per variant site, not
nucleotide diversity; only the "All positions (variant and fixed)" block is
per sequenced site.

To check your own Stacks version, take a row of `populations.sumstats.tsv`
and confirm `Pi` = `Exp_Het` × 2*N*/(2*N* − 1) and `Fis` = (`Pi` −
`Obs_Het`)/`Pi`. `diversity_core_selftest()` checks these against rows of
published Stacks output.

## Appendix B. How other tools compare

Checked against the named versions; later versions may differ.

| | RADdiversity | hierfstat 0.5.11 | diveRsity (GitHub source) | Stacks 2.68 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| He estimator | Nei & Chesser | Nei & Chesser (`basic.stats`) | plug-in 1 − Σ*p*<sup>2</sup> | 2*N*-corrected `Pi` |
| FIS over loci | ratio of sums | ratio of sums (`basic.stats` overall) | not checked | mean of per-site ratios |
| resampling unit | RAD loci (individuals for `_se_ind`) | loci as rows (`boot.ppfis`, `boot.ppfst`, `boot.vc`) | individuals (`divBasic`) | none; SD/√sites |
| rarefied private richness | yes, with SE | no | no | no |
| FST at records typed in one population | skipped | kept (`wc`) | — | skipped |
| global D at records missing a population | skipped | — | — | — |
